\begin{document}

\begin{abstract}
  A worked example built on the electrochemical degradation of a pharmaceutical pollutant: the
  molecule, the reaction at the anode, and the kinetics, all regenerated from the files in
  \texttt{data/} whenever they change.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Atenolol reaches wastewater treatment plants largely unchanged, and anodic oxidation is one of
the processes studied for removing it.\cite{moragomez2020} The molecule is shown in
Figure~\ref{fig:atenolol}; its structure was drawn from a single SMILES string, itself obtained
from the systematic name with \texttt{labharness resolve}.

\begin{figure}
  \centering
  \labfigure{figures/atenolol.pdf}
  \caption{Atenolol, drawn by RDKit from \texttt{data/atenolol.smi}.}
  \label{fig:atenolol}
\end{figure}

\section{Results and discussion}

At the anode surface, water is oxidised to a sorbed hydroxyl radical, which then attacks the
aromatic ring of the pollutant (Figure~\ref{fig:mechanism}). The scheme is written in TikZ and
chemfig, which is what makes the curved arrows possible: they are drawn, not approximated.

\begin{figure}
  \centering
  \labfigure{figures/mechanism.pdf}
  \caption{Hydroxyl radical generation at the anode and attack on the aromatic ring.}
  \label{fig:mechanism}
\end{figure}

The relative concentration decays as $C/C_0 = a\,e^{bt}$ (Figure~\ref{fig:decay}), with
$b = \FitDecayB \pm \FitDecayBError$ min$^{-1}$; the apparent rate constant is its magnitude.
The fit is exponential rather than a straight line through
the logarithms, so the rate constant is not biased by the transformation.

\begin{figure}
  \centering
  \labfigure{figures/decay.pdf}
  \caption{Relative concentration against time, with a first-order fit. Demonstration data.}
  \label{fig:decay}
\end{figure}

The apparent rate constant grows linearly with the applied current density
(Figure~\ref{fig:kapp}), at \FitKappSlope{} $\pm$ \FitKappSlopeError{} min$^{-1}$ per
mA~cm$^{-2}$, which is what is expected when the oxidising species are produced in proportion
to the current. None of these numbers is typed into this text: they are written by the scripts
that draw the figures, so they follow the data.

\begin{figure}
  \centering
  \labfigure{figures/kapp.pdf}
  \caption{Apparent rate constant against applied current density. Demonstration data.}
  \label{fig:kapp}
\end{figure}

A second, unrelated scheme is included here to show that a mechanism can be asked for and
drawn on the spot: the acid-catalysed iodination of acetone (Figure~\ref{fig:iodination}), where
the rate-determining enolisation is what makes the reaction zero order in iodine.

\begin{figure}
  \centering
  \labfigure{figures/iodination.pdf}
  \caption{Acid-catalysed iodination of acetone. The slow step is the enolisation.}
  \label{fig:iodination}
\end{figure}

\section{Conclusions}

Change a number in \texttt{data/decay.csv} and save: the figure, the fit and the rate constant
quoted above all follow, and the PDF reloads on its own.
